# Preface {.unnumbered}

This textbook on multilevel and longitudinal models is written for applied researchers in education and the social sciences. It grew out of the course *S-043: Multilevel and Longitudinal Models* at the Harvard Graduate School of Education. The content is primarily based on Josh Gilbert's S-043 lecture slides when he taught the course in Fall 2026. Bill Young turned the slides into detailed lecture notes which form the foundation of this text. Josh then used AI tools to convert Bill's notes into this online format and further edited the content. Thus, Josh and Bill are equal contributors to this work.

::: callout-warning
## Work in progress

This is a draft and will be updated over time.
:::

## Who this book is for

Readers who are comfortable with ordinary regression and want to know what changes when observations come in groups: students in schools, patients in hospitals, repeated measures in people. We assume familiarity with R, but the focus is on what the models *mean* rather than syntax or mathematical derivations.

## How each chapter is organized

Every chapter follows the same structure:

- **The chapter in one paragraph.** The whole argument, before the details.
- **The main text.** Built around a single running example, with every equation tied to R code and every number in the output used in a sentence.
- **Vocabulary decoder and common mistakes.** The field uses many names for the same thing; these sections sort them out.
- **Quick reference.** The formulas in one place.
- **Worked examples and self-check.** Questions with answers hidden until you want them.

## Software

Almost all models are fit in R with `lme4`:

``` r
install.packages("lme4")
library(lme4)
```
